newsitem.title: POLAND: Fragile Polish zloty waits for foreign orders.
newsitem.headline: Fragile Polish zloty waits for foreign orders.

text.p: The zloty, wary after losing nearly two percent since last Wednesday amid foreign investor withdrawal from Polish instruments, closed little changed on Monday as London and New York financial markets were closed.
Dealers said however that foreign orders could materialise as world markets open on Tuesday and again pit the zloty's fall against the central bank currency-selling interventions.

"There could be some orders tomorrow...but the zloty is not likely to fall much because the NBP will likely prop it up through interventions," said Tomasz Nowakowski, forex dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
The zloty closed at 0.68/0.59 percent from the trading band centre, a touch up from Friday's all-time low against the currency basket at 0.64/0.50 percent.
It closed at 3.2060/90 to the dollar, up from 3.2120/65 on Friday and at 1.8995/10 to the mark, flat from 1.8992/19.
Dealers said the market was very cautious with one-figure spreads remaining for much of today's session and with sums as small as $20 million having a large impact on the market.
They said foreigners, who last week rushed to cut Central European exposure after the Czech crown's decline, may reduce Polish positions more slowly to keep the zloty from falling.

"It seems that not all foreigners who wanted to withdraw already did so, but any sales are likely to be spread out over time as not to put excessive downward pressure on the zloty," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.
At Monday's tender the treasury sold 945 million zlotys of T-bills and kept the minimum prices of most bills unchanged.
Foreigners showed little interest in the auction, buying only minute amounts of bills on Monday, dealers said.
The benchmark 52-week T-bill minimum price eased 0.03 point to 82.18, driving up the average yield to 21.40 percent.
The shortest 8-week paper's minimum price inched up 0.01 to 96.85 from the last auction on April 28, with the average yield forming at 20.77 percent.
One-day rates fell below 21 percent as the money market's surplus liquidity was not absorbed by central bank drainage operations on Monday, dealers said.
Overnight and tomorrow/next rates both fell half a point to close at 20.75/21.00 and 20.80/21.00 percent respectively.
